The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index fell to 47.8 in early September 2026, down for a second consecutive month and well below market expectations of 51.0, according to the preliminary estimate.

It was the weakest reading since May’s record low.

results.content: Consumer sentiment is also now lower than at any point during Biden's presidency. The University of Michigan's preliminary September 2026 reading was 47.8, compared to 70.1 just two years prior under Biden in September 2024, and around 30 points under his peak of 79.0 in January of that year. It was also lower than Biden's previous low, a then-historic 50.0 in June 2022. [...] The University of Michigan's preliminary September survey found consumer sentiment fell to 47.8, down from 51.7 in August and 13.2 percent below its level a year earlier. The reading was the second lowest in the survey's history if confirmed in the final report.

results.content: The preliminary September University of Michigan consumer sentiment index registered 47.8, falling well short of the 51.0 market consensus and breaking below the 50 threshold. This marks the lowest level since May, when the index hit its record low. Inflation expectations released simultaneously rose across the board, underscoring the deterioration in a key indicator closely watched by the Federal Reserve. [...] The preliminary September University of Michigan consumer sentiment index came in at 47.8, sharply below the 51.0 consensus estimate and the lowest reading since May. One-year inflation expectations jumped to 4.6%, the highest since June, while 5-10 year expectations climbed to 3.4%.

results.content: Consumer sentiment plunged in September amid heightened inflation fears, hitting its second-lowest level on record in the University of Michigan’s monthly survey released Friday. The survey’s headline index hit a level of 47.8, down 7.5% from the August reading and off 13.2% from a year ago. This was the second-lowest reading on record for data going back to 1952 — the bottom coming in May as rising prices also jolted the outlook. Indeed, the one-year inflation outlook surged to 4.6%, up 0.6 percentage point from the prior level and the highest since hitting the same level in June.
